newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's health forces would-be heirs to wait.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's health forces would-be heirs to wait.

text.p: A year after Boris Yeltsin was elected for a second term as Russia's president, friends and foes alike are manoeuvring for the right to succeed him.

Yeltsin, who has been in power since 1991 and was reelected on July 3 last year, is barred from seeking a third term under the constitution and has not named a preferred successor for the election scheduled for the year 2000.
The 66-year-old leader's recovery after health problems makes him more likely to see out his term now than had appeared likely several months ago, before he underwent heart surgery.
But some politicians appear to have one eye on the election with almost every move they make, and are courting the financial and political allies they will need to launch a campaign.
Much will depend on who wins the approval of the president, the powerful Kremlin machine behind him and the influential media and financial groups who favoured Yeltsin last year.

Possible candidates at this early stage include ousted security aide Alexander Lebed, Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov and rising reformer Boris Nemtsov. Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov and liberal Grigory Yavlinsky may also run for a second time.
"If the election were held right now, Lebed would probably be the favourite, but in the long run I would probably bet on Luzhkov at the moment," political analyst Andrei Kortunov said.
"On the other hand, Lebed came from almost nowhere to finish third in last year's election and it is possible that someone else could appear on the scene."
Lebed, 47, appealed to Russians who want a strong hand in the Kremlin by running on a law and order ticket.

Yeltsin appointed him his top security aide after the first round to clinch the run-off against Zyuganov. Lebed signed the deal which ended nearly 21 months of fighting in Chechnya but was sacked last October for harbouring presidential ambitions.

Lebed remains popular but has the disadvantages of having no major political party or financial backers behind him. His criticism of almost all Yeltsin's moves make him appear impatient and overtly ambitious, and could soon wear thin.

Luzhkov, 60, did not run in the last election and has carefully nurtured good ties with Yeltsin. He was elected for a second mayoral term last year with a huge majority and is seen as a man who gets things done.

Luzkhkov's main weakness is that his powerbase is limited to Moscow. But he has been trying to boost his appeal outside the capital by travelling often and speaking out on a host of issues beyond his brief, although he has not said he plans to run.
He could also be helped by the fact that the Moscow region recently won the right to its own national television channel.

"Everything Luzhkov is doing is intended to strengthen his position in readiness for a presidential bid and the television channel is a vital part of his election armour," said one political source, who declined to be named.

Nemtsov, 37, has emerged as a contender since Yeltsin persuaded him in March to give up his job as a regional governor and become a first deputy prime minister with an important role to play in reforms.
He is the golden boy of Russian politics, and many political analysts regard his decision to take on his tough government job as a clear signal that he has presidential ambitions.
But the young liberal has likened his new post to a suicide mission and he does not yet have a strong powerbase among the influential financial and political elites in the capital.
"He needs to build up his support in Moscow and this could be very difficult for him," Kortunov said.
Zyuganov appears not to have enough appeal to be elected and the Communist Party's chances are widely dismissed unless it changes policies under a more charismatic leader.
Yavlinsky, who was ousted in last year's first round, is an outside challnger and stolid Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is thought to lack popular appeal if he decides to run.

Powerful government reform chief Anatoly Chubais, who masterminded Yeltsin's reelection win, is regarded by most politicians and analysts as too unpopular to become president, but could have a decisive say in Yeltsin's choice of heir.
